topics.title: Memory Areas
topics.description: What lives where in a running JVM, and which flag sizes it.

areas.title: Heap
areas.description: All objects and arrays. Shared across threads. Sized with -Xms (initial) and -Xmx (max).

areas.title: Young generation
areas.description: New objects land in Eden. Survivors of a minor GC are copied between the survivor spaces S0 and S1, and are eventually promoted to the old generation after surviving enough cycles (the tenuring threshold).

areas.title: Old generation
areas.description: Long-lived objects. Collected by major or full GC, which is more expensive.

areas.title: Metaspace
areas.description: Class metadata; replaced PermGen in Java 8. Grows in native memory, capped with -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize.

areas.title: Thread stacks
areas.description: One per thread, sized with -Xss. Holds frames with local variables and partial results. Throws StackOverflowError when exceeded.

topics.title: Generational GC
topics.description: Most objects die young. Every mainstream collector is built to exploit that.

collection_types.title: Minor GC
collection_types.description: Collects only the young generation. Frequent, fast, copies few survivors.

collection_types.title: Major / Full GC
collection_types.description: Includes the old generation, and possibly metaspace. Slower, and historically stop-the-world.

collection_types.title: Stop-the-world (STW)
collection_types.description: Application threads are paused while GC works. Modern collectors minimize STW pauses.

topics.how_reclamation_works: The JVM tracks reachability from GC roots: thread stacks, static fields, JNI references. Unreachable objects are reclaimed. G1 and ZGC do most of that work concurrently to keep pauses short.
topics.minor_vs_major_in_one_line: Minor collects the young generation only, fast and frequent. Major or full includes the old generation — in older collectors a long stop-the-world event, while G1 and ZGC avoid full GCs unless degraded.

topics.title: GC Algorithms
topics.description: Pick by pause target, not by fashion. G1 is the default since Java 9 and is the right answer for most services.

rows: Batch jobs where total throughput beats latency
Large heaps (multi-GB to TB), low-latency APIs. Generational ZGC is the default ZGC mode since Java 23
Similar niche to ZGC, mainly Red Hat builds

topics.g1_in_one_paragraph: The answer interviewers want: G1 divides the heap into equal-sized regions of 1 to 32 MB. Each region acts as Eden, survivor or old as needed. It marks live objects concurrently, then evacuates the regions with the most garbage first — hence Garbage First — giving predictable pauses controlled by -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis.
topics.zgc_over_g1: Choose ZGC for latency-critical services with large heaps where even 100-200 ms pauses hurt: trading, real-time APIs. The trade-off is slightly more CPU and memory overhead. For typical CRUD services default G1 is fine — saying so shows judgment.

topics.title: Tuning Flags
topics.description: The flags worth knowing by heart, plus the container rule that catches people out.

common_flags.code:
-Xms4g -Xmx4g              # fixed heap avoids resize pauses; common in containers
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100   # G1 pause goal
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps
-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log      # unified GC logging (Java 9+)
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0  # container-aware sizing instead of -Xmx

topics.container_awareness: Since Java 10 the JVM reads cgroup limits. In Kubernetes use MaxRAMPercentage rather than hardcoding -Xmx.
topics.forcing_gc: System.gc() is only a hint, and is often disabled with -XX:+DisableExplicitGC. You cannot deterministically force a collection, and a design should never depend on it.

topics.title: OOM Diagnosis
topics.description: Naming the right OutOfMemoryError variant, and the leak that caused it, is most of the answer.

error_types.title: OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
error_types.description: The heap is exhausted — either a leak or an undersized heap.

error_types.title: OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace
error_types.description: Too many classes, often a classloader leak.

error_types.title: OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread
StackOverflowError
error_types.description: Deep or unbounded recursion. Not an OutOfMemoryError, but the distinction is the point.

debug_flow: Enable a heap dump on OOME: -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
Analyze retained sizes in Eclipse MAT
Look for the dominator holding the memory
classic_leak_causes: ThreadLocal not removed in thread pools

topics.title: Troubleshooting
topics.description: Symptom to tool, so you can name the command instead of describing it vaguely.

rows: jmap -dump or -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError, then Eclipse MAT or VisualVM — look at the dominator tree and retained size
jstack <pid> several times, find hot threads by matching top -H thread id to hex to stack
GC logs via -Xlog:gc*, read in GCEasy or GCViewer
jcmd — one tool for dumps, VM flags and native memory: jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory
Java Flight Recorder: jcmd <pid> JFR.start — low overhead, analyze in JDK Mission Control

topics.title: Class Loading
topics.description: Three phases, and one delegation rule that explains why you cannot replace java.lang.String.

phases.title: 1. Loading
phases.description: Bytes become a Class object, through the Bootstrap, Platform and Application classloader hierarchy.

phases.title: 3. Initialization
phases.description: Static initializers run, lazily, on first active use.

topics.parent_delegation: A classloader asks its parent first, which prevents user code replacing java.lang.String. Breaking delegation deliberately is how app servers and plugin systems isolate versions.

topics.title: JIT Compilation
topics.description: Bytecode starts interpreted; hot methods get compiled.
topics.tiered_compilation: Hot methods are compiled by C1 (client) and then C2 (server). That escalation is what tiered compilation means.
optimizations: Escape analysis — may allocate on the stack or eliminate locks
topics.why_it_matters: Warm-up affects benchmarks, which is why microbenchmarks need JMH rather than a System.nanoTime() loop.

topics.title: Reference Types
topics.description: The four reachability strengths and what each one is for.

references.title: Strong
references.description: Normal references. Never collected while reachable.

references.title: Soft
references.description: Collected only under memory pressure. Used for caches.

references.title: Weak
references.description: Collected at the next GC once only weakly reachable. Used by WeakHashMap and canonical maps.

references.title: Phantom
references.description: Enqueued after finalization, for cleanup hooks. Cleaner uses these, replacing finalize() which is deprecated for removal.
